subChunks.title: CRUD Operations & Filtering
subChunks.hookHtml: The Academy's records don't live in code — they live in tables. SQL is the language every Java engineer must speak: how to store data, retrieve it with precision, and keep it consistent.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is SQL?

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for relational databases. You write declarative statements that describe what you want — the database engine decides how to fetch it.

Core CRUD Operations

-- CREATE a table
CREATE TABLE spells (
    id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name    VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    tier    VARCHAR(20),
    damage  INTEGER DEFAULT 0
);

-- INSERT rows
INSERT INTO spells (id, name, tier, damage)
VALUES (1, 'Fireball', 'APPRENTICE', 80),
       (2, 'Frostbolt', 'JUNIOR', 120),
       (3, 'Thunderwave', 'SENIOR', 200);

-- SELECT all
SELECT * FROM spells;

-- SELECT with filter
SELECT name, damage FROM spells WHERE tier = 'JUNIOR';

-- UPDATE
UPDATE spells SET damage = 90 WHERE name = 'Fireball';

-- DELETE
DELETE FROM spells WHERE damage < 100;

Filtering and Ordering

-- Multiple conditions
SELECT * FROM spells WHERE damage > 100 AND tier != 'APPRENTICE';

-- Pattern matching
SELECT * FROM spells WHERE name LIKE 'Fire%';

-- Ordering
SELECT * FROM spells ORDER BY damage DESC;

-- Limiting results
SELECT * FROM spells ORDER BY damage DESC LIMIT 3;

-- Aggregate functions
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM spells;
SELECT AVG(damage), MAX(damage), MIN(damage) FROM spells;
SELECT tier, COUNT(*) AS spell_count FROM spells GROUP BY tier;

Transactions

A transaction groups multiple operations — either all succeed (COMMIT) or all fail (ROLLBACK):

BEGIN;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
-- If either UPDATE fails, ROLLBACK undoes both

storyBeats.text: The Academy's records room contains a crystalline database — every spell ever cast, every apprentice ever enrolled, every transaction ever made. The records keeper speaks SQL fluently, pulling any information in seconds.

storyBeats.speaker: Records Keeper Dalynn
storyBeats.text: SQL has four fundamental operations: SELECT to read, INSERT to add, UPDATE to change, DELETE to remove. These are CRUD — Create, Read, Update, Delete. Every web application you will ever build uses them thousands of times per minute.

storyBeats.speaker: Basic CRUD on spells table
storyBeats.text:
-- Read all spells above damage 100:
SELECT name, damage FROM spells
WHERE damage > 100
ORDER BY damage DESC;

-- Result:
-- name        | damage
-- Thunderwave | 200
-- Frostbolt   | 120

storyBeats.speaker: Records Keeper Dalynn
storyBeats.text: WHERE filters rows. AND and OR combine conditions. LIKE lets you match patterns — 'Fire%' matches anything starting with Fire. ORDER BY sorts results. GROUP BY aggregates. And transactions ensure that when you transfer mana from one account to another, both sides change or neither does.

learningObjectives: Write SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements for a single table
Filter results using WHERE with AND, OR, and LIKE
Sort and limit results with ORDER BY and LIMIT
Use aggregate functions COUNT, AVG, MAX, MIN and GROUP BY
Explain what a transaction is and why COMMIT/ROLLBACK matter
commonMistakes: Writing UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause — updates/deletes ALL rows
Confusing = with == in SQL — equality in SQL always uses a single =
Using HAVING instead of WHERE to filter individual rows — HAVING filters groups
Forgetting that NULL is not equal to anything, including NULL — use IS NULL, not = NULL
assessmentCriteria: Can write a SELECT with multiple WHERE conditions, ORDER BY, and LIMIT
Can write an UPDATE that changes a specific row and explain why a missing WHERE is dangerous
Can use GROUP BY with COUNT to produce a summary table
Can explain what a transaction provides and give a real-world scenario where rollback is essential
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain SQL CRUD operations to someone who has never used a database. What does each operation do? Why are transactions important, and what would go wrong without them?

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Create a new table mages with columns: id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), level INTEGER, school VARCHAR(50). Insert 4 mages of your choice with levels between 1 and 10. Then write queries to: (a) select all mages with level >= 5, (b) find the average level, (c) select the name and level of the highest-level mage.

questions.questionHtml: Which SQL clause filters rows in a SELECT statement?
questions.explanationHtml: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY. ORDER BY sorts results. GROUP BY aggregates rows into groups.

questions.questionHtml: A developer runs: UPDATE spells SET damage = 999;. What is the consequence?
questions.correctAnswer: Every row in the spells table has its damage set to 999 — the missing WHERE clause applies the update to all rows
questions.explanationHtml: UPDATE without WHERE is one of the most dangerous SQL mistakes. Always include a WHERE clause when updating specific rows. In production, databases often have safeguards (like requiring a WHERE clause), but you cannot rely on them.

questions.questionHtml: You need to find all spells whose name contains 'bolt' anywhere. Which is correct?
questions.explanationHtml: LIKE is the SQL pattern-matching operator. % matches any sequence of characters. So '%bolt%' matches any string that contains 'bolt' anywhere. = requires an exact match.

subChunks.title: Joins & Normalisation
subChunks.hookHtml: A single table can only hold one entity's worth of information. Real systems have dozens of related tables — mages, spells, assignments, schools. JOINs are how you stitch those tables back together into meaningful answers.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Foreign Keys

A foreign key in one table references the primary key in another, creating a relationship:

CREATE TABLE mages (
    id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100)
);
CREATE TABLE spell_assignments (
    mage_id  INTEGER REFERENCES mages(id),
    spell_id INTEGER REFERENCES spells(id)
);

JOIN Types

-- INNER JOIN: only rows that match in both tables
SELECT m.name, s.name AS spell
FROM mages m
INNER JOIN spell_assignments sa ON m.id = sa.mage_id
INNER JOIN spells s ON sa.spell_id = s.id;

-- LEFT JOIN: all rows from left table + matching rows from right (NULL if no match)
SELECT m.name, s.name AS spell
FROM mages m
LEFT JOIN spell_assignments sa ON m.id = sa.mage_id
LEFT JOIN spells s ON sa.spell_id = s.id;
-- Includes mages with no assigned spells (spell column = NULL)

Normalisation in Brief

Normalisation is the process of structuring tables to reduce redundancy. The key rule: each piece of information should live in exactly one place.

  • 1NF: Each column holds a single value (no lists in a cell), each row is unique
  • 2NF: Every non-key column depends on the whole primary key, not part of it
  • 3NF: No non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependencies)

Practical test: if you can update a piece of information in one row and not in another (because it's duplicated), your schema is not normalised.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's records span multiple ledgers — one for mages, one for spells, one for assignments. The records keeper retrieves information from all three simultaneously with a single statement.

storyBeats.speaker: Records Keeper Dalynn
storyBeats.text: Separate tables prevent duplication. A mage's name lives in one place. A spell's damage lives in one place. JOIN brings them together at query time without duplicating the data. INNER JOIN gives you only rows with matches on both sides. LEFT JOIN includes all rows from the left table even if there's no match on the right.

storyBeats.speaker: Join mages with their spells
storyBeats.text:
SELECT m.name AS mage, s.name AS spell, s.damage
FROM mages m
INNER JOIN spell_assignments sa ON m.id = sa.mage_id
INNER JOIN spells s ON sa.spell_id = s.id
ORDER BY s.damage DESC;

-- Shows every mage-spell pairing, sorted by damage

storyBeats.speaker: Records Keeper Dalynn
storyBeats.text: Normalisation is the discipline behind this separation. If a mage's school name appears in every spell_assignment row, updating it requires touching every row — and forgetting even one creates an inconsistency. Store it once in the mages table. Reference it everywhere else.

learningObjectives: Write an INNER JOIN query connecting two tables via a foreign key
Explain the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN
Define first, second, and third normal form in plain terms
Identify a denormalised schema and describe what should be split into a separate table
commonMistakes: Forgetting the ON clause in a JOIN — produces a cartesian product (every combination of every row)
Using INNER JOIN when you need LEFT JOIN — mages with no spells are silently excluded
Storing comma-separated values in a column (e.g. 'spell1,spell2,spell3') — violates 1NF
Aliasing tables with long names in complex JOINs makes queries unreadable — use short aliases like m, s, sa
assessmentCriteria: Can write a two-table JOIN with correct ON condition and table aliases
Can explain what data is returned by INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN for the same query
Can identify a repeated data pattern in a schema and propose a normalised alternative
Can explain why foreign keys enforce referential integrity
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain SQL JOINs to someone who has never seen them. Use a physical analogy — like a reference table in a library — to illustrate why we have separate tables at all, and what INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN returns.

Propose a normalised schema (write the CREATE TABLE statements for at least two tables), then write a JOIN query that produces the same information as the original table.

soloPracticeTests.label: Two or more normalised tables defined

options: All rows from the left table and matching rows from the right
Only rows where there is a match in both tables
All rows from the right table and matching rows from the left
questions.correctAnswer: Only rows where there is a match in both tables
questions.explanationHtml: INNER JOIN returns only rows where the join condition matches in both tables. Rows with no match in either table are excluded. Use LEFT JOIN to keep all rows from the left table regardless of whether a match exists.

questions.questionHtml: A developer writes SELECT * FROM mages, spells;. How many rows are returned if mages has 10 rows and spells has 20 rows?
questions.correctAnswer: 200 rows — this is a cartesian product (every mage combined with every spell), caused by missing a JOIN...ON condition
questions.explanationHtml: Without an ON condition, the comma join produces every possible combination: 10 × 20 = 200 rows. This is almost never what you want. Always write an explicit JOIN with an ON clause.
